findings.excerpt: fn job_by_key(&self, key: &str) -> Result<Option<JobRow>, MetaError> {   [consumer: ag-server/src/api/jobs.rs:133 `tx.job_list(None, 1000)?.into_iter().find(|j| j.dedupe_key.as_deref() == Some(&key))`]
findings.problem: The dedupe lookup is private, so the server emulates it by scanning the newest 1000 jobs. Once a validation job is older than the 1000 newest, the scan misses it, the enqueue path falls through to job_enqueue (which does dedupe in storage) but also emits the 'enqueued' metric and a second job.enqueue audit event for work that was not enqueued.
findings.proposed_fix: Make it `pub fn job_by_dedupe_key` (indexed by the UNIQUE dedupe_key) and use it in ag-server instead of the capped scan; add a server test with >1000 jobs asserting no duplicate audit event.
reasons: Confirmed: ag-server/src/api/jobs.rs:133 looks for an existing job with `tx.job_list(None, 1000)...find(dedupe_key == key)`, but the real lookup `Tx::job_by_key` (meta/jobs.rs:218) is private, and I found no code that prunes the jobs table. Once the matching job is outside the newest 1000, the scan misses it. job_enqueue_with still returns the stored job, but the server then increments the 'enqueued' metric and appends a spurious 'job.enqueue' audit entry. This is reachable via the proposal-validation route.

Confirmed: job_by_key is private (jobs.rs:218), and ag-server/src/api/jobs.rs:133 emulates it with `tx.job_list(None, 1000)...find(dedupe_key)`. When the existing job is older than the 1000 newest, the scan misses it. job_enqueue then dedupes in storage and returns the old job, but the server still counts an 'enqueued' metric and appends a false job.enqueue audit entry. existing_validation_jobs has the same cap (500) and under-reports.
findings.refined_fix: In crates/ag-storage/src/meta/jobs.rs rename `fn job_by_key` to `pub fn job_by_dedupe_key(&self, key: &str) -> Result<Option<JobRow>, MetaError>` (update its caller inside job_enqueue_with). In crates/ag-server/src/api/jobs.rs:133 replace the `tx.job_list(None, 1000)?.into_iter().find(...)` with `let existing = tx.job_by_dedupe_key(&key)?;`. Add a server test that enqueues one validation job, creates more than 1000 other jobs, re-requests validation, and asserts that no second 'job.enqueue' audit entry appears.

findings.excerpt: scope: serde_json::from_str(&scope_json).unwrap_or_default(),
findings.problem: A credential whose stored scope_json cannot be parsed silently gets the default CredentialScope, which Scope::from_wire/Scope::permits treat as UNRESTRICTED (empty repos/streams/operations = any). A damaged row or schema drift therefore widens a narrowly scoped agent credential to everything its subject's roles allow. Fail-open swallowed error in the authentication path.
findings.proposed_fix: Make row_to_credential return rusqlite::Error::FromSqlConversionFailure on a parse error so Authenticator::authenticate fails closed (log the credential id, answer unauthenticated/internal). Add CHECK (json_valid(scope_json)) to the credentials table. Add an integration test that corrupts scope_json in a real control.db and asserts the token is rejected, never accepted unrestricted.
reasons: Control::credential_from (now crates/ag-server/src/control/mod.rs:306, the file was split from control.rs) really does `serde_json::from_str(r.str(5)?).unwrap_or_default()`, and Authenticator::authenticate_token (auth/mod.rs:228-254) feeds that row into Scope::from_wire, where empty lists mean unrestricted (authz.rs is_unrestricted/permits). The row is written only via serde, but Control::import (control/dump.rs:355-363) inserts scope_json from a backup file without validation, so a bad or hand-edited backup or a damaged row silently widens a credential. Practical severity is medium because it needs DB damage or a bad restore.

The file is now crates/ag-server/src/control/mod.rs:306 and still has `scope: serde_json::from_str(r.str(5)?).unwrap_or_default()`. A default CredentialScope has empty lists, which Scope::from_wire/is_unrestricted/permits treat as unrestricted, and authenticate_token (auth/mod.rs:254) uses it with no check. dump.rs import (355-366) also writes scope_json without validating it. Proto types are serde(default) without deny_unknown_fields, so version skew does not trigger this; only genuinely damaged JSON does, but fail-open in the auth path is still wrong.
findings.refined_fix: In control/mod.rs `credential_from`, replace the `unwrap_or_default()` with `scope: serde_json::from_str(r.str(5)?).map_err(|e| MetaError::Corrupt(format!("credential scope_json does not parse: {e}")))?`. `db()` turns that into ApiError::internal, so authenticate_token and still_active fail closed through their existing `??`. In `credentials()` (the listing), skip and `tracing::error!` a corrupt row instead of failing the whole listing. In `Control::import` (control/dump.rs) parse every `scope_json` and `quota_json` as `v1::CredentialScope` / `v1::Quota` before the INSERTs and return `MetaError::Invalid` on failure. Add a unit test in control/mod.rs that writes `scope_json = 'not json'` with `db.execute`, then asserts `credential(id)` is Err and that authenticate_token rejects the token. A `CHECK (json_valid(...))` constraint is optional and needs a new 0003 migration for both SQLite and Postgres.

findings.excerpt: quota: serde_json::from_str(&quota).unwrap_or_default(),
findings.problem: An unparsable quota_json silently becomes the default Quota, i.e. every limit 0 = unlimited (object bytes, streams, open proposals, per-repo rate limit). A corrupt row disables all quota enforcement for that repository without any signal.
findings.proposed_fix: Propagate the parse error (FromSqlConversionFailure) and refuse to serve the repository with a logged internal error; add CHECK (json_valid(quota_json)); test with a corrupted row.
reasons: Control::repo_from (control/mod.rs:450) has `serde_json::from_str(r.str(6)?).unwrap_or_default()`. repo()/repos() back repo_row(), which feeds store_object, create_stream, create_proposal and the repo rate limiter, and a default Quota means every limit is 0 = unlimited (proto: '0 = unlimited'). A malformed quota_json, for example from an unvalidated import in control/dump.rs:380-389, therefore silently disables enforcement.

control/mod.rs:450 `quota: serde_json::from_str(r.str(6)?).unwrap_or_default()` turns an unreadable quota_json into Quota::default(), where 0 means unlimited. Every quota (object bytes, streams, proposals, per-repo rate limit) is then silently disabled with no log. Impact is lower than finding 0, since only real corruption can trigger it.
findings.refined_fix: In `repo_from`, use `quota: serde_json::from_str(r.str(6)?).map_err(|e| MetaError::Corrupt(format!("repo quota_json does not parse: {e}")))?`, so that a repo with a corrupt quota answers `internal` and is logged rather than served unlimited. In `repos()` (used by list_repos and rebuild_job_index) skip and log corrupt rows so one bad row cannot break the listing for everyone. Validate `quota_json` in `Control::import` as in finding 0. Add a test with a corrupted row that expects an error rather than `Quota::default()`.

findings.excerpt: control.add_object_bytes(&name, size as i64)?;
findings.problem: The repository object quota (quota.max_total_object_bytes) is checked and accounted ONLY in App::store_object (the object upload path). add_object_bytes has no other caller. Blobs and changesets written through virtual workspaces (api/workspaces.rs:112 workspace_modify with inline VirtualContent::Bytes), and everything else that writes through the engine, are neither counted nor limited, so a writer can exceed the quota arbitrarily with repeated /workspaces/{name}/changes calls (8 MiB per request, unlimited requests). Docs advertise repository quotas as done (docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:89). object_bytes is also never reconciled except by a manual non-dry-run GC (admin.rs:146).
findings.proposed_fix: Enforce the quota where bytes actually enter the repository: account and check in workspace_modify/modify_workspace (and any other writer) or, better, in a quota-aware wrapper around the repository's ObjectStore so every put is counted. Add periodic reconciliation (set_object_bytes from objects().list()) instead of GC-only. Verify with a real-server test that uploads through the workspace API past max_total_object_bytes and expects quota_exceeded.
reasons: object_bytes is charged and checked only in App::store_object (api/objects.rs:88-125); a grep shows add_object_bytes has no other caller and set_object_bytes is only called by non-dry-run GC (api/admin.rs:146). api/workspaces.rs to_change turns inline FileChange.content into VirtualContent::Bytes, and ag-integrate virtual_ws.rs:69 `change_to_target` stores it with put_blob, so repeated /workspaces/{name}/changes calls write unlimited blobs past max_total_object_bytes. docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:89 nevertheless marks repository quotas as done.

add_object_bytes is called only from App::store_object (api/objects.rs:125). modify_workspace -> repo.workspace_modify -> self.commit (ag-integrate/src/virtual_ws.rs:112-146) writes inline blobs and changesets with no quota check or accounting. A writer can therefore exceed max_total_object_bytes through the workspace API. The only reconciliation is a non-dry-run GC (admin.rs:146). docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:89 and the existing test (tests/security.rs repository_quotas_are_enforced) cover only the upload path.
findings.refined_fix: Factor the quota check and accounting out of store_object into `App::charge_object_bytes(&self, repo: &str, delta: u64) -> ApiResult<()>`. It should read the RepoRow, return QuotaExceeded when `max_total_object_bytes > 0 && object_bytes + delta > max`, then call `control.add_object_bytes`. Call it from modify_workspace and sync_workspace before `repo.workspace_modify` / `workspace_sync_virtual`, with delta = the sum of `VirtualContent::Bytes` lengths in the request (an upper bound is fine, since accounting is documented as approximate). A sturdier alternative is to wrap the repository's ObjectStore so every put is counted. Reconcile `set_object_bytes` from `repo.objects().list()` periodically, not only in GC. Add a real-server test that pushes past the quota through /workspaces/{name}/changes and expects `quota_exceeded`.

findings.excerpt: max_object_bytes: 0,
findings.problem: Quota.max_object_bytes (proto field 2, accepted by PATCH /v1/repos/{owner}/{rname} and stored/returned) is never enforced anywhere: objects.rs:41 and http.rs:402 use only the global cfg.limits.max_object_bytes. default_quota also hardcodes max_object_bytes/max_streams/requests_per_second/burst to 0 and config.rs only offers defaults for max_open_proposals and max_total_object_bytes, so operators cannot set a default for the other quota fields.
findings.proposed_fix: Enforce the per-repo max_object_bytes in ObjectSink::push and store_object (use min(global, repo quota)); add [limits] defaults for max_object_bytes, max_streams, requests_per_second and burst and use them in default_quota; test through the real HTTP server.
reasons: Quota.max_object_bytes is accepted by configure_repo and stored, but a grep shows production code only reads cfg.limits.max_object_bytes (objects.rs:41, http.rs:421, session.rs:40), never `quota.max_object_bytes`. `default_quota` (api/repository.rs:31-39) hardcodes max_object_bytes, max_streams, requests_per_second and burst to 0, and LimitsSection (config.rs) has defaults only for max_open_proposals and max_total_object_bytes.

Quota.max_object_bytes is accepted and stored by configure_repo, and the Web UI SettingsPanel.vue offers it as 'Largest object (bytes) - 0 = server default'. Nothing enforces it: objects.rs:41 and http.rs:421 use only cfg.limits.max_object_bytes, and grep shows no other reader of quota.max_object_bytes. An operator who sets it gets a silent no-op. The part about missing [limits] defaults for the other quota fields is a feature request, not a defect.
findings.refined_fix: In store_object, extend the quota tuple to `(max_total, max_object, used)` and, before storing, reject with `ErrorCode::TooLarge` when `max_object > 0 && size > max_object`. In `upload_sink`, fetch the RepoRow once and store `min(cfg.limits.max_object_bytes, per-repo max_object_bytes if > 0)` in ObjectSink so `push` enforces it per chunk. Add `max_streams`, `requests_per_second` (repo) and `burst` (repo) defaults to LimitsSection, wire them into `default_quota`, and add a real-HTTP test.

findings.excerpt: if max_streams > 0 && repo.meta().read(|tx| tx.list_streams())?.len() as u32 >= max_streams {
findings.problem: Quota checks are check-then-act and not atomic: max_streams (here), max_open_proposals (proposals.rs:27-28, which also loads up to 100_000 rows to count) and the object quota (objects.rs:88-111, where used bytes are read outside the write and before authorization) all race under concurrent requests, so quotas can be exceeded. Documented as 'approximate' only for object_bytes.
findings.proposed_fix: Perform the count and the insert in one metadata transaction (or a SQL-level conditional insert) so the quota is enforced atomically; for object bytes use an atomic reserve (UPDATE ... SET object_bytes = object_bytes + ?2 WHERE object_bytes + ?2 <= max) before writing and roll back on failure.
reasons: create_stream (api/streams.rs:36-45) reads max_streams, lists the streams and then creates the stream in separate steps, and create_proposal (api/proposals.rs:16-28) counts open proposals via `proposals_list(Some("open"), 100_000)` before inserting. with_repo/with_repo_mut (app.rs:404-446) run closures on concurrent spawn_blocking threads with no per-repo lock, and store_object reads `object_bytes` outside the write, so concurrent requests can exceed all three quotas. Impact is low (quotas overshoot by the concurrency level).

The check-then-act race is real in create_stream (streams.rs:42), create_proposal (proposals.rs:27) and store_object (objects.rs:88-105), but the overshoot is bounded by in-flight concurrency. No unbounded growth results, unlike the workspace bypass in finding 2. control/mod.rs:120 already documents object_bytes as 'approximate'. Exact atomic reservation is best handled as part of the finding 2 fix, not as a separate defect.
findings.refined_fix: Do the count and the insert in one `repo.meta().write(|tx| ...)` transaction, which the metadata write lock serialises per repository. For streams: inside the write, `if max_streams > 0 && tx.list_streams()?.len() as u32 >= max_streams { return Err(QuotaExceeded) }` and then create the stream in the same transaction. Do the same for proposals, using a COUNT query instead of loading 100_000 rows. For object bytes, replace the read-then-add with one conditional statement, `UPDATE repos SET object_bytes = object_bytes + ?2 WHERE name = ?1 AND (?3 = 0 OR object_bytes + ?2 <= ?3)`, and check the affected-row count before writing.

findings.excerpt: WHERE (?1 IS NULL OR subject = ?1) AND (?2 IS NULL OR repo = ?2) ORDER BY subject, repo, role LIMIT 5000",
findings.problem: all_bindings() (the source of every authorization decision) calls roles(None, None), which silently truncates at 5000 rows ordered by subject. The comment says 'Bindings are few' but nothing enforces it: bindings beyond the 5000th (late subjects alphabetically) are silently ignored, so those users are denied or get not_found with no error. Same pattern: credentials() LIMIT 1000 (line 248) silently truncates list_credentials and the may_manage_credential scan; all_bindings (line 324) also silently drops rows with an unknown role via filter_map.
findings.proposed_fix: Give all_bindings its own unlimited query (or fail loudly when more rows than a documented, configurable cap exist) and log/skip-with-warning on unknown roles; paginate credentials/roles listings with page tokens instead of a hidden LIMIT. Test with 6000 bindings against a real control.db.
reasons: Control::roles (control/mod.rs ~line 337) ends in `ORDER BY subject, repo, role LIMIT 5000`, and all_bindings() (the cache source for every authorize call via App::bindings) calls `roles(None, None)` and drops unknown roles with filter_map, so binding 5001 onward is silently ignored. credentials() has a hidden `LIMIT 1000` used by list_credentials and may_manage_credential. The comment 'Bindings are few' is not enforced anywhere.

control/mod.rs:413-421 all_bindings() calls roles(None,None), whose SQL has `ORDER BY subject, repo, role LIMIT 5000` (line 396). Bindings past the 5000th are silently dropped, so later subjects get not_found or permission_denied with no error. One binding per user per repo reaches 5000 in a mid-size OIDC org. The unknown-role filter_map also drops silently. The claim that may_manage_credential scans credentials() is wrong: it takes a single row, and revoke_credential uses credential(id). Only the list_credentials 1000-row cap is a valid, lesser point.
findings.refined_fix: Give all_bindings its own query, `SELECT subject, repo, role FROM roles` with no LIMIT. Log with `tracing::warn!` every row whose role fails `Role::parse` instead of dropping it silently. For list_roles and list_credentials, add page tokens or at least return a `truncated` indication instead of a hidden cap. Add a test that inserts 6000 bindings into a control.db and asserts that the 6000th is honoured by `App::bindings()`.

findings.excerpt: || (!inner.is_empty() && inner.raw().iter().all(|p| outer.matches(p) || outer.raw().contains(p)))
findings.problem: Scope::contains decides whether a delegated credential's pattern is a subset of its minter's by matching the inner pattern's SOURCE TEXT as a literal string against the outer glob. That is not glob inclusion and is unsound: outer repos=['acme/*b*'] 'contains' inner ['acme/[ab]*'] because the literal text 'acme/[ab]*' matches 'acme/*b*', yet the inner pattern also matches 'acme/alpha', which the outer does not. A narrowly scoped token can therefore mint a wider one, breaking the 'a credential can never exceed its minter' guarantee (docs/protocol/agwp-v1.md). The same literal-pattern-as-repo-name trick is used for CredentialsMint/CredentialsRevoke checks in api/admin.rs:200 and :259.
findings.proposed_fix: Replace with a real containment check: restrict scope patterns to a decidable grammar (literal segments with a single trailing '*' or a bare '*') validated at mint time, and implement prefix/segment containment on that grammar; reject character classes, '?', '{}' in scopes and bindings. For admin checks, verify the minter's role pattern contains the requested pattern with the same function. Add property tests comparing against brute-force enumeration over a name universe.
reasons: Scope::contains (authz.rs) accepts an inner pattern if `outer.matches(p)`, i.e. it matches the inner pattern's source text as a string. With outer 'acme/*b*' and inner 'acme/[ab]*', the text 'acme/[ab]*' matches the outer glob (it contains a 'b'), yet the inner glob also matches 'acme/alpha', which the outer does not. mint_credential (api/admin.rs:200-224) uses this, and a self-mint (subject == own principal) has no other check, so a narrowly scoped token can mint a wider one. The same literal-text trick is used in the CredentialsMint check in mint_credential and the CredentialsRevoke check in may_manage_credential.

authz.rs:305-313 Scope::contains matches the inner pattern's source text against the outer glob. I ran globset 0.4.20: outer `acme/*b*` matches the literal text `acme/[ab]*`, so contains() returns true, yet the inner pattern matches `acme/alpha` and the outer does not. mint_credential (admin.rs:191) therefore lets a narrowly scoped token mint a wider one, contradicting 'never more powerful than their minter' in docs/protocol/agwp-v1.md. It needs a mid-string wildcard in the outer scope, so common `prefix/*` scopes stay sound, but it is still an unsound security check.
findings.refined_fix: In authz.rs add `fn simple(p: &str) -> bool { !p.is_empty() && p.bytes().enumerate().all(|(i, b)| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b"._-/".contains(&b) || (b == b'*' && i == p.len() - 1)) }` and `pub fn pattern_within(outer: &str, inner: &str) -> bool { if outer == "*" || outer == inner { return true; } if !simple(outer) || !simple(inner) { return false; } match outer.strip_suffix('*') { Some(prefix) => inner.trim_end_matches('*').starts_with(prefix), None => false } }`. Rewrite `list_ok` in Scope::contains as `outer.is_empty() || (!inner.is_empty() && inner.raw().iter().all(|p| outer.raw().iter().any(|o| pattern_within(o, p))))`, and drop the `outer.matches(p)` path. Reject non-simple patterns for newly minted scopes in mint_credential and admin mint only, so stored credentials still authenticate. In mint_credential and may_manage_credential, replace the `Authorizer::check(me, &bindings, p, ...)` calls on pattern text with a check that some binding whose role grants the capability and whose subject matches the caller has `pattern_within(&binding.repo, p)`. Add a property test against brute-force enumeration over a name universe.

findings.excerpt: Glob::new(pattern).map(|g| g.compile_matcher().is_match(value)).unwrap_or(false)
findings.problem: An invalid glob in a stored role binding silently never matches. Bindings are not validated on creation: api/admin.rs:335-337 (grant_role) only checks the role and that subject is non-empty, and main.rs:213-214 (admin grant) validates nothing, so typos create permanently inert bindings that look granted in list_roles. The glob is also recompiled for every binding on every request.
findings.proposed_fix: Validate subject and repo patterns (Patterns::new / Glob::new plus subject shape user:/agent:/service:/group:) in Control::grant_role and the API, return invalid_argument; cache compiled matchers inside the bindings cache.
reasons: api/admin.rs grant_role validates only the role and a non-empty subject, and main.rs `AdminAction::Grant` validates only the role, so an invalid glob can be stored. `glob_match` (authz.rs) returns false on Glob::new errors, so such a binding is inert but still shown by list_roles. `Authorizer::roles` calls glob_match, which compiles a new Glob, for every binding on every authorize. The failure mode is safe (fail-closed) but a confusing typo trap, and the per-request recompilation is wasteful.

grant_role in api/admin.rs:328-344 checks only the role name and a non-empty subject, and the CLI Grant path (main.rs:414-417) validates nothing. I confirmed `Glob::new("acme/[")` fails, and glob_match (authz.rs:240-242) turns a compile error into false. A typo therefore returns success and is listed in list_roles, but never grants anything. The per-request recompilation of every binding's glob is a secondary performance point.
findings.refined_fix: Add `pub fn validate_pattern(p: &str) -> Result<(), String> { globset::Glob::new(p).map(|_| ()).map_err(|e| format!("bad pattern '{p}': {e}")) }` in authz.rs. Call it for subject and repo in App::grant_role (return ApiError::invalid) and in the main.rs `Grant` branch. In `App::bindings()` cache compiled `GlobMatcher`s next to each Binding (a struct `CompiledBinding { binding, subject: GlobMatcher, repo: GlobMatcher }`) so `Authorizer::roles` stops calling Glob::new per request.

findings.excerpt: let mut cfg = ServerConfig::default();
findings.problem: The offline `ag-server admin` command builds its App from ServerConfig::default() and has no --config flag, so it ignores the real configuration. `admin create-repo` therefore always creates SQLite+filesystem repositories even when the server is configured with [repos.storage] PostgreSQL/S3 (the shipped compose setup), producing repositories the server would later open with the wrong backend/layout; it also ignores repos.default_stream and the limits.* quota defaults (main.rs:245 passes v1::Quota::default()), and the auth ttl caps.
findings.proposed_fix: Add --config/AG_SERVER_CONFIG to `admin` and load the same ServerConfig as `serve`; use the repository defaults (default_quota, default_stream, storage template) in create-repo. Verify against the compose PostgreSQL/MinIO stack that `admin create-repo` yields a repo in its own schema/prefix.
reasons: The headline claim is stale: Command::Admin now has `--config`/AG_SERVER_CONFIG and copies repos, control and data_dir from the loaded config (main.rs ~211-216), and tests/admin_config.rs covers the storage template (commit 499c922), so the PostgreSQL/S3 backend claim no longer holds. The remaining parts still hold. `cfg.limits` and `cfg.auth` are not copied from the loaded config, `CreateRepo` passes `v1::Quota::default()` instead of the API's default_quota, and `--default-stream` has a hard `default_value = "main"` that overrides `repos.default_stream`. So repos created by `admin create-repo` get no configured quota defaults and the wrong default stream.

The headline claims are stale. `ag-server admin` now has --config/AG_SERVER_CONFIG and copies repos, control and data_dir from the loaded config (main.rs:49-58, 249-257), so create-repo uses the configured PostgreSQL/S3 storage template. The residual is real: cfg.limits is not copied and create-repo passes `v1::Quota::default()` (main.rs:447) instead of default_quota() (limits.max_total_object_bytes/max_open_proposals). The `--default-stream` flag also defaults to 'main' rather than repos.default_stream. Repos created offline therefore silently miss the operator's default quotas.
findings.refined_fix: This is narrowed to the leftovers; the --config flag already exists. In the Admin branch also set `cfg.limits = loaded.limits; cfg.auth = loaded.auth;`. Make `default_stream` an `Option<String>` on `CreateRepo` and use `default_stream.unwrap_or_else(|| app.cfg.repos.default_stream.clone())`. Make `App::default_quota` `pub` (api/repository.rs:31) and call `app.default_quota()` instead of `v1::Quota::default()`. Add a test in tests/admin_config.rs with `[limits] max_total_object_bytes = 123` and `[repos] default_stream = "trunk"` that creates a repo offline and checks both.

findings.excerpt: expires_at_ms: now + i64::from(ttl) * 1000,
findings.problem: `admin mint` accepts any u32 ttl (default 3600, up to ~136 years) and never applies auth.max_ttl_secs / auth.max_agent_ttl_secs that the API enforces (api/admin.rs:217-224), contradicting the docs ('always expiring', agents <= 1 h). Combined with the default-config issue above the caps cannot even be read.
findings.proposed_fix: Load the config in admin and apply the same per-kind max TTL as App::mint_credential (share one function).
reasons: `AdminAction::Mint` in main.rs sets `expires_at_ms: now + i64::from(ttl) * 1000` for any u32 ttl and never applies auth.max_ttl_secs / max_agent_ttl_secs, which App::mint_credential enforces (api/admin.rs:217-224). The claim that the caps cannot be read is outdated, because --config exists, but the Admin branch never copies `loaded.auth`. The documented 30-day service tokens (docs/guides/orchestrator.md uses --ttl 2592000) equal the default max_ttl_secs, so enforcing the caps does not break documented usage. Severity is low because the caller already has DB-level access.

`admin mint` is the offline operator tool with direct database authority. --ttl is an explicit flag (default 3600) and the credential is always expiring. The [auth] max-TTL caps are policy for API callers. Note that the Admin branch does not even load cfg.auth. An operator who passes a huge --ttl knows what they typed, so nobody is misled, and the docs say agents are 'at most 1 h by default'.
findings.refined_fix: In the Admin config load add `cfg.auth = loaded.auth;`. In `AdminAction::Mint`, after building `identity`, add `let max = if identity.kind() == ag_types::IdentityKind::Agent { app.cfg.auth.max_agent_ttl_secs } else { app.cfg.auth.max_ttl_secs }; if ttl > max { bail!("--ttl may be at most {max}s for {} credentials (auth.max_ttl_secs / auth.max_agent_ttl_secs)", identity.kind().prefix()); }`. Better, share one `fn clamp_ttl(cfg: &AuthSection, kind, ttl) -> Result<u32, String>` between App::mint_credential and the CLI. Also reject `ttl == 0`.

findings.excerpt:
meta_backend: "sqlite".into(),
        object_backend: "fs".into(),
        durability: String::new(),
        stream_count: 0,
        changeset_count: 0,
findings.problem: row_to_wire fills canned values: backend names 'sqlite'/'fs' and zero stream/changeset counts and empty durability. create_repo and every entry of list_repos return these as if true, even for repositories on PostgreSQL/S3 (only describe_repo overwrites them at lines 124-128). Clients (Web UI repo list, SDKs) see wrong backends and 0 streams/changesets.
findings.proposed_fix: Derive meta_backend/object_backend from the effective storage template (cfg.repos.storage / the repo's stored config) in row_to_wire, and either compute counts for listings or make the fields optional/omitted when not computed (do not emit 0). Test with a Postgres/S3 repo in tests/storage_backends.rs asserting list and create report the real backends.
reasons: row_to_wire (api/repository.rs:21-27) hardcodes meta_backend 'sqlite', object_backend 'fs', empty durability and zero counts. create_repo returns it (line 83) and stores it as the idempotent result, and list_repos maps every row through it. Only describe_repo overwrites the fields from the live repo (lines 124-128). A PostgreSQL/S3 repo is therefore reported as sqlite/fs on create and list. RepoRow.config_json already holds the real storage template.

api/repository.rs:21-26 row_to_wire hardcodes meta_backend 'sqlite' and object_backend 'fs', and create_repo and list_repos return it unchanged. Only describe_repo overwrites it (lines 124-128). proto/agwp.proto documents the counts as 'Filled by Describe only', so zero counts are legitimate. The backend names are documented as 'Storage in use' and are wrong for PostgreSQL/S3 repos. dev/handoff/release.md already records this as 'Not fixed'.
findings.refined_fix: Derive the backends in row_to_wire from `r.config_json`: `let (m, o) = serde_json::from_str::<ag_integrate::RepoConfig>(&r.config_json).map(|c| { let s = c.storage(); (if matches!(s.meta, ag_integrate::MetaConfig::Postgres { .. }) { "postgres" } else { "sqlite" }, if matches!(s.objects, ag_integrate::ObjectsConfig::S3 { .. }) { "s3" } else { "fs" }) }).unwrap_or(("sqlite", "fs"));` and set meta_backend/object_backend from it. Leave stream_count/changeset_count/durability empty in list and create, and document them as 'only filled by GetRepo' in the proto comment. Add a case to tests/storage_backends.rs asserting that list and create report postgres/s3.

findings.excerpt: pub public_url: Option<String>,
findings.problem: Documented as 'Externally visible base URL (for links in responses and OIDC redirects)' but it is never read anywhere in the repository (only declared and defaulted); no response contains links and there are no OIDC redirects (the server validates bearer tokens only). A dead configuration knob advertising features that do not exist; openapi.json also hardcodes servers [{"url":"/"}] (routes.rs:263).
findings.proposed_fix: Either remove the field (deny_unknown_fields will then reject stale configs) or implement it: use it for the OpenAPI servers entry, absolute links and the OIDC redirect login flow planned in the web product, and validate it as an absolute http(s) URL.
reasons: `public_url` appears only at config.rs:70 (declaration) and :89 (default None) in the main tree and in the worktrees. Nothing reads it: routes.rs:263 emits a fixed `"servers": [{"url": "/"}]` and there is no OIDC redirect code. The doc comment advertises links and OIDC redirects that do not exist, and deny_unknown_fields means operators may set it and expect an effect.

ServerSection.public_url is documented as 'Externally visible base URL (for links in responses and OIDC redirects)'. Grep across crates, deploy, docs and apps finds it only at config.rs:70 and :89, so it is never read. The OIDC redirect login in ui.rs takes its redirect URI from [[ui.login]], not from public_url. It is a dead knob accepted silently, so an operator can set it expecting behaviour that does not exist.
findings.refined_fix: Smallest honest fix: remove the field, its doc comment and `public_url: None` from ServerConfig/Default, since no doc or deploy config references it. If the OIDC redirect login (web track) will use it, keep it and add a check in `ServerConfig::validate` that it parses as an absolute http(s) URL without a trailing path, and pass it to `routes::openapi` so the `servers` entry uses it when set.

findings.excerpt: const MAX_MESSAGE: usize = 16 * 1024 * 1024;
findings.problem: gRPC decode/encode size is a fixed 16 MiB, unrelated to the configurable limits.max_request_bytes (default 8 MiB) that the HTTP transport honours (http.rs:100) and that Negotiate advertises (session.rs:41). Lowering max_request_bytes does not restrict gRPC; raising it above 16 MiB has no effect on gRPC while clients are told otherwise.
findings.proposed_fix: Pass cfg.limits.max_request_bytes (and chunk-size aware limits for ObjectService) into router() and use it for max_decoding/encoding_message_size; test that a gRPC request above the configured limit gets too_large.
reasons: grpc.rs:31 sets `MAX_MESSAGE = 16 MiB`, and router() (line ~608) applies it to max_decoding_message_size and max_encoding_message_size for every service. The HTTP transport uses cfg.limits.max_request_bytes (http.rs:100), and Negotiate advertises that value (api/session.rs:41). Changing limits.max_request_bytes therefore has no effect on gRPC.

grpc.rs:31 and :608 apply a fixed 16 MiB max_decoding_message_size to every service. limits.max_request_bytes is described as the largest non-streaming request body, is advertised by Negotiate (session.rs:41) and is honoured only by HTTP (http.rs:100). An operator who lowers it to cap memory leaves gRPC accepting 16 MiB messages. The impact is small, since the default HTTP limit is 8 MiB and object chunks are 1 MiB, but the configured limit does not apply to one transport.
findings.refined_fix: In `grpc::router(app)` compute `let decode = (app.cfg.limits.max_request_bytes as usize).max(ag_protocol::limits::CHUNK_BYTES + 64 * 1024);` and use `.max_decoding_message_size(decode)` in the svc! macro. Keep the encoding limit a separate named constant, because responses such as tree pages are not bounded by the request limit. Add a gRPC test where limits.max_request_bytes is small and an oversized unary request returns `too_large` (ResourceExhausted).

findings.excerpt:
max_changeset_ops: 100_000,
                max_changesets_per_publication: 10_000,
findings.problem: Negotiate advertises engine limits as duplicated literals instead of reading them from the engine (ag_types::Limits::default() has the same numbers today, so they can silently drift). The engine limits themselves are not configurable by an operator: ag-integrate/src/repo.rs:140 uses Limits::default() for every repository, so max_ops, max_dag_depth, max_tree_entries, max_blob_size etc. cannot be tuned from [limits].
findings.proposed_fix: Add the engine Limits to the server config ([limits.engine]) and pass them into Repository::open; build the Negotiate limits from that same value (single source of truth) and add a test that the advertised and enforced values agree.
reasons: api/session.rs:44-45 advertises `max_changeset_ops: 100_000` and `max_changesets_per_publication: 10_000` as literals, while the engine enforces ag_types::Limits::default() (ag-integrate repo.rs:140), whose fields have the same values today. Two sources of truth can drift, and the advertised limits are the client contract. This is minor; making the engine limits operator-configurable is a feature request, not a defect.

The literals in Negotiate (100_000 ops, 10_000 changesets per publication) equal ag_types::Limits::default() (ag-types/src/limits.rs), which every repository uses via Repository::assemble. Engine limits are fixed data-model and format limits (DAG depth, tree entries, ops per changeset). Making them per-server tunable would risk repositories that are not portable between servers. There is no current mismatch, only a hypothetical drift.
findings.refined_fix: In `negotiate`, use `let engine = ag_types::Limits::default();` with `max_changeset_ops: u32::try_from(engine.max_ops).unwrap_or(u32::MAX)` and `max_changesets_per_publication: u32::try_from(engine.max_changesets_per_publication).unwrap_or(u32::MAX)`. Add a unit test that compares them with the limits of an open Repository (`repo.limits()`).

findings.excerpt: if Authorizer::roles(p, std::slice::from_ref(b), &b.repo.replace('*', "x")).contains(&b.role) {
findings.problem: whoami computes the caller's roles by replacing '*' in each binding's repo pattern with the literal 'x' and testing that fake repository name. This is wrong for patterns with '?', character classes or alternation (a binding like 'acme/{web,api}' or 'acme/[ab]' never matches its own substituted text), so the reported role list silently omits roles the caller really holds, and it can include roles that only apply to a different name.
findings.proposed_fix: Report bindings that apply to the principal by matching on the SUBJECT only (subject_ok in Authorizer::roles) and return the repo pattern as stored; do not synthesize a repository name.
reasons: whoami (api/session.rs:57) tests each binding against `b.repo.replace('*', "x")`. For repo patterns with '?', character classes or alternation, such as 'acme/{web,api}' or 'acme/[ab]', the substituted literal does not match its own pattern, so a role the caller really holds is omitted from the Principal.roles list returned by session.whoami.

whoami only affects an informational role list. The `replace('*', "x")` trick is exact for the documented `*`-only patterns. I confirmed with globset that `acme/{web,api}` and `acme/[ab]` do not match their own text, so classes and alternation are omitted. Neither is documented as supported grammar, and no authorization decision uses this output.
findings.refined_fix: In authz.rs extract the subject test from `Authorizer::roles` into `pub fn subject_matches(p: &Principal, subject: &str) -> bool { let base = p.identity.principal(); glob_match(subject, p.identity.as_str()) || glob_match(subject, base.as_str()) || p.groups.iter().any(|g| subject == format!("group:{g}")) }` and use it in both places. In whoami push `format!("{}:{}", b.repo, b.role.as_str())` for every binding where `subject_matches(p, &b.subject)`, with no fake repo name.

findings.excerpt: .unwrap_or(Outcome::Invalid { reason: format!("operation is {} and has no result yet", i.state) });
findings.problem: For an integrate operation without a (parsable) stored result, GetOperation fabricates an IntegrationOutcome with status 'invalid' and a prose reason. A pending/in-flight operation or a result that fails to deserialize (error swallowed by .ok() on line 302) is reported to clients as a terminal 'invalid' outcome rather than as pending/unknown, which breaks the documented 'ask for the outcome after deadline_exceeded' protocol.
findings.proposed_fix: Return outcome: None with the operation state ('pending'/'applying') when there is no result, and an internal error (logged with request id) when a stored result fails to parse; add a test that polls an operation mid-flight.
reasons: api/convert.rs:299-303 builds the 'integrate' operation outcome with `.and_then(|v| serde_json::from_value::<Outcome>(..).ok()).unwrap_or(Outcome::Invalid { reason: format!("operation is {} and has no result yet", ..) })`. A not-yet-finished operation, or a stored result that fails to parse (the error is swallowed by `.ok()`), is therefore reported as a terminal `invalid` outcome, although the proto allows an absent outcome and `state` carries the real state. GetOperation is the route clients poll after deadline_exceeded.

The engine does exactly this (ag-integrate/src/integrate.rs:185-187), and the convention is deliberate. The response also carries the real lifecycle `state` (pending/applying/...) next to the outcome, and the reason text says 'operation is {state} and has no result yet', so the message is truthful. No handwritten SDK or UI code reads outcome.status to detect completion. A stored result that fails to parse requires corruption.
findings.refined_fix: Replace the fabricated outcome. Use `let outcome = match i.result.as_ref() { None => None, Some(v) => match serde_json::from_value::<Outcome>(v.clone()) { Ok(o) => Some(self::outcome(&o)), Err(e) => { tracing::error!(operation = %i.operation_id, error = %e, "stored integration result does not parse"); None } } };` and set `op.integration = Some(v1::IntegrationResult { operation_id: i.operation_id.clone(), state: i.state.to_string(), outcome })`. Change `convert::operation` to return ApiResult if a parse failure should surface as `internal`. Add a test that polls an operation while it is prepared/applying.

findings.excerpt: Ok((tx.audit_after(after_seq, limit.saturating_mul(4).max(limit))?, latest))
findings.problem: Topic-filtered event reads fetch only 4*limit raw audit rows and then filter. subscribe() (lines 137-140: 'else if batch.latest_seq > st.cursor { st.cursor = batch.latest_seq; }') treats an empty filtered window as 'only filtered-out events arrived' and jumps the cursor to the latest sequence, permanently skipping matching events that lie beyond the 1024-row window (e.g. a burst of >1024 non-matching audit entries followed by a matching one). replay() returns a short/empty page that clients read as 'no more events'. This violates the documented 'loses nothing' resume guarantee.
findings.proposed_fix: Push the topic filter into the audit query (WHERE action matches) or loop until `limit` matching events are found or the log is exhausted, and only advance the cursor to the last row actually examined. Add a test with >1024 non-matching entries between matching events through a real server.
reasons: events_after (api/events.rs:61) reads only `limit*4` raw audit rows after the cursor (1024 for subscribe's limit of 256) and then applies the topic filter. When none of those rows match, subscribe (lines 137-142) takes `else if batch.latest_seq > st.cursor { st.cursor = batch.latest_seq }`, which skips over every unexamined row, including matching ones beyond the window. replay() likewise returns a short or empty page that does not say whether the log is exhausted. The module doc promises that resuming 'loses nothing'.

events.rs:61 reads only max(4*limit, limit) raw audit rows and then filters by topic. In subscribe() (lines 150-155), when no event in that window matches but latest_seq > cursor, the cursor jumps to latest_seq. Matching events beyond the window are skipped permanently; for example, with 1,500 non-matching audit rows before a matching one and a 256-event limit, the window is 1,024 rows and the matching row is lost. replay() returns an empty page that clients read as the end. This breaks the module doc's 'resumes with after_seq and loses nothing'.
findings.refined_fix: Add `next_after: u64` to EventBatch (the highest seq actually examined). In events_after, loop inside one `meta().read` over `tx.audit_after(cursor, 1024)` pages, advancing `cursor = last row seq` and collecting matching events until `limit` events are found or a page has fewer than 1024 rows, and set `next_after` to the last examined seq. In subscribe replace the `else if batch.latest_seq > st.cursor` branch with `if batch.next_after > st.cursor { st.cursor = batch.next_after; }`. Let replay report `next_after` so clients can continue. Add a test with more than 1024 non-matching audit entries followed by a matching one, run through a real server.

findings.excerpt: app.cfg.server.cors_origins.iter().filter_map(|o| HeaderValue::from_str(o).ok()).collect();
findings.problem: Invalid CORS origins are silently dropped; if every entry is invalid the layer allows nothing and browser clients fail with no diagnostic. ServerConfig::validate does not check cors_origins. Allowed methods/headers and max_age(600) are fixed.
findings.proposed_fix: Validate cors_origins in ServerConfig::validate (absolute origin, no path, or '*' explicitly) and fail startup on a bad entry; optionally make max_age configurable.
reasons: server.rs `cors()` builds the origin list with `filter_map(|o| HeaderValue::from_str(o).ok())`, so invalid entries vanish silently, and ServerConfig::validate (config.rs:361-435) has no check on server.cors_origins. If all entries are bad the layer allows nothing and browsers fail with no diagnostic. The fixed allowed methods/headers/max_age are fine as they are.

server.rs:87-88 only drops origins that fail HeaderValue::from_str (control characters), which is rare. Typical typos such as a missing scheme or trailing slash pass through and simply never match, so the layer fails closed and the browser console reports the CORS error. Fixed methods, headers and max_age(600) are sensible defaults for an optional feature. This is a nice-to-have validation, not an operator-hurting defect.
findings.refined_fix: In ServerConfig::validate add `for o in &self.server.cors_origins { if axum::http::HeaderValue::from_str(o).is_err() || !(o.starts_with("http://") || o.starts_with("https://")) || o[o.find("://").unwrap() + 3..].contains('/') { return bad(&format!("server.cors_origins: '{o}' must look like https://host[:port] (scheme and host, no path)")); } }`, and make `cors()` use the validated list unchanged. Add a unit test for a bad entry.

findings.problem: Empty branch that evaluates a condition and does nothing; dead code that reads like a missing check. The same file has a redundant branch in list_credentials (line 283: `if out.is_empty() && subject != "*" && subject != me { return Ok(...out) }` followed by an identical Ok(...)) whose comment claims special privacy handling that does not exist.
findings.proposed_fix: Delete both branches (or implement the intended check) and add tests proving self-minting only narrows and that listing another subject's credentials reveals nothing.
reasons: Both branches exist as described. api/admin.rs:210-212 `else if me.scope.is_unrestricted() && ... { /* comment only */ }` is a no-op in a security-sensitive function, and the `if out.is_empty() && subject != "*" && subject != me { return Ok(..out) }` in list_credentials is followed by an identical Ok(..out), while its comment claims privacy handling. Behaviour is unaffected (may_manage_credential already filters), so this is a cleanup, but misleading dead code in an authorization path is worth removing.

I confirmed the empty `else if` at admin.rs:210-212 and the redundant identical return at 283-286. Both are dead code with no behavioural effect: list_credentials already filters every row through may_manage_credential, so nothing is revealed. This is a cosmetic cleanup, not a defect that hurts or misleads an operator.
findings.refined_fix: Delete the empty `else if` branch in mint_credential, keeping the explanatory comment above the `if !own` block ("self-minting is always allowed; Scope::contains already guarantees it can only narrow"). Delete the redundant early `if out.is_empty() ... return` in list_credentials and keep the single `Ok(v1::ListCredentialsResponse { credentials: out })`. Add a test that lists another subject's credentials without admin rights and gets an empty list.

findings.excerpt: //! Each caller (credential, falling back to identity) has a token bucket;
findings.problem: The doc says the bucket falls back to identity, but App::rate_limit (app.rs:320) always keys on 'cred:{credential_id}'. For OIDC tokens the id is the per-token jti, so one user minting/refreshing tokens gets a fresh full bucket each time (limit bypass) and the bucket map grows; for the bootstrap token everyone shares one bucket. Unauthenticated/failed-auth traffic is never rate limited (limiting runs after authentication), and the pre-auth /v1/capabilities route bypasses dispatch entirely (no limiting or shedding).
findings.proposed_fix: Key the limiter on the principal identity (optionally also per credential) as documented, rate limit failed authentications per remote address, and route negotiate through the concurrency gate.
reasons: App::rate_limit (app.rs ~371) always keys the bucket on `format!("cred:{}", credential_id)`, contrary to the limits.rs doc ('credential, falling back to identity'). Because each credential has its own full bucket, a caller can multiply its allowance by self-minting credentials via mint_credential (each new one starts with a full burst) or, for OIDC, by presenting different tokens (credential_id is the per-token jti, oidc.rs:~213). Authentication failures are never rate limited because limiting happens after authenticate. The pre-auth /v1/capabilities route is intentionally outside dispatch.

app.rs:373 keys the limiter on the credential id, and the docs describe 'per-credential rate limits' (docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:89), so behaviour matches the documented contract. The module comment 'falling back to identity' is slightly loose, but there is no operator harm. Obtaining many OIDC tokens requires going through the IdP, and bucket growth is bounded by the idle eviction. Rate limiting of unauthenticated traffic is a feature request, and concurrency is already bounded by the semaphore.
findings.refined_fix: Key the main limiter on the principal, not the credential: `let key = format!("id:{}", call.principal.identity.principal());` in App::rate_limit, with the bootstrap principal keeping its own key. Use the same identity-based key in repo_rate_limit (`id:{principal}|repo:{repo}`). Optionally keep the per-credential bucket as a second, smaller check. Add a failed-authentication limiter keyed by remote address once finding 31 provides it. Add a test where a caller mints N credentials and the combined rate stays at the identity's limit.

findings.excerpt:
const KEY_REFRESH_MIN_INTERVAL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30);
const KEY_MAX_AGE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(3600);
findings.problem: JWKS refresh interval/max age (24-25), the 10 s HTTP timeout for discovery and JWKS (line 80) and the clock-skew leeway (`validation.leeway = 30`, line 185) are fixed and not configurable per provider. load_jwks also holds the key-cache mutex across the blocking network call, so one slow identity provider stalls every OIDC authentication.
findings.proposed_fix: Add per-provider jwks_refresh_secs, http_timeout_secs and leeway_secs to [[auth.oidc]] and fetch the JWKS outside the lock (singleflight).
reasons: The tunable-constants part is not a defect, but the concurrency issue is real. In auth/oidc.rs `key_for` takes `self.cache.lock()` and calls `self.refresh(&mut cache)`, which runs the blocking ureq discovery and JWKS fetches (10 s timeout each) while the guard is held. Even cache hits for the same provider wait on that mutex, so one slow identity provider stalls every OIDC authentication on blocking-pool threads.

Only the lock behaviour is a defect; the fixed constants are named, sensible defaults. In oidc.rs key_for (131-150) the per-provider cache Mutex is held across refresh(), which does blocking ureq discovery plus JWKS fetches with 10 s timeouts each. A failed refresh does not set `fetched`, so while the IdP is slow or down every request carrying a JWT with a matching unverified `iss` retries the refresh in turn under the lock, and these requests queue on blocking-pool threads (no rate limit applies before authentication). Once the cache is older than 1 h (KEY_MAX_AGE), even cached keys are not used.
findings.refined_fix: Take the lock only to read the cache. Add `refresh_gate: Mutex<()>` to the provider. In `key_for`: (1) lock the cache, return the key if fresh and found, unlock; (2) otherwise lock `refresh_gate`, recheck under the cache lock (another thread may have refreshed, or KEY_REFRESH_MIN_INTERVAL has not passed), and if a refresh is still needed call `let set = self.load_jwks()?` with no cache lock held; (3) re-lock the cache briefly, install the keys, set `fetched`, and look up. Only refreshers wait on the gate, and cached lookups are never blocked by network I/O.

findings.excerpt: /// W3C `traceparent`, passed through to logs.
findings.problem: Neither Ingress.traceparent nor the trace id reaches the logs: the per-request span (app.rs:207) records only op, request_id and transport. docs/protocol/agwp-v1.md:68 repeats the claim ('`traceparent` is propagated into logs and traces'); only the OTLP exporter uses it.
findings.proposed_fix: Add trace_id (from the incoming or newly sampled context) to the request log span, or correct the docs and the field comment.
reasons: The comment at app.rs:42 ('W3C traceparent, passed through to logs') and docs/protocol/agwp-v1.md:66 ('`traceparent` is propagated into logs and traces') are only half true. Ingress.traceparent is consumed solely by `tracer.begin()` (app.rs:254), and the per-request log span (app.rs:257) records only op, request_id and transport. No trace id reaches the logs, so log lines cannot be correlated with exported traces.

Ingress.traceparent is documented 'passed through to logs' (app.rs:42), and docs/protocol/agwp-v1.md:66 says '`traceparent` is propagated into logs and traces'. The per-request log span (app.rs:257) records only op, request_id and transport, and traceparent is consumed only by tracer.begin (line 254). Operators therefore cannot correlate logs with trace ids as the protocol doc promises. docs/operations/observability.md describes only trace propagation, so it is the protocol doc and the field comment that are wrong.
findings.refined_fix: In `dispatch`, declare the log span as `info_span!("request", op, request_id = %ing.request_id, transport = ing.transport, trace_id = tracing::field::Empty)`. After `tracer.begin`, record `hex::encode(ctx.trace_id)` into it; when the tracer is disabled, record the trace-id segment parsed from the incoming traceparent (the second `-`-separated field). Alternatively, correct the field comment and agwp-v1.md:66 to 'propagated into traces'.

findings.excerpt:
/// Peer address, for logs.
    pub remote: Option<String>,
findings.problem: Ingress.remote is never read by anything (not logged, not audited), and for HTTP it is always None (http.rs:61 callers pass None; the ConnectInfo<SocketAddr> service wiring in server.rs:208/212 is never extracted). Failed authentications and audit entries therefore carry no source address.
findings.proposed_fix: Extract ConnectInfo<SocketAddr> (and optionally a trusted X-Forwarded-For allow-list) in the HTTP handlers, include remote in the request log span and in auth-failure warnings.
reasons: Ingress.remote is documented 'Peer address, for logs' (app.rs:44-45), but a grep shows nothing ever reads `.remote`. For HTTP every handler calls `ingress_from_headers(&headers, None)` (http.rs:187, 269, 292, 418, 450, 646, 1254, 1300), even though server.rs serves with `into_make_service_with_connect_info::<SocketAddr>()`. gRPC fills it (grpc.rs:68) but never uses it. Failed-auth warnings and audit entries therefore carry no source address.

Confirmed that Ingress.remote is never read (grep finds only its definition and construction), and HTTP passes None. It is a documented-in-comment convenience field, not a promised feature in any user doc, and the server is usually behind a proxy. Logging the peer address is an enhancement, not a defect.
findings.refined_fix: Add the `axum::extract::ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>` extractor to the HTTP handlers (or one `from_fn` middleware that stores the address in request extensions) and pass `Some(addr.to_string())` instead of `None`. In `dispatch` add `remote = ing.remote.as_deref().unwrap_or("-")` to the request log span, and include it in the `auth_failures` warning (app.rs:302-304). Optionally honour X-Forwarded-For only from a configured trusted-proxy list.

findings.excerpt: //! Server configuration (TOML file + environment overrides).
findings.problem: There are no environment overrides of configuration values: the environment supplies only secrets (bootstrap/metrics/OTLP-header tokens) and AG_SERVER_CONFIG/AG_DATA_DIR/AG_HEALTHCHECK_URL for the CLI. validate() also misses several settings: telemetry.log_format (anything other than 'json' silently means text, main.rs:109), limits.burst = 0 with a rate set (silently 1), repos.default_stream (only fails later on every create_repo), cors_origins, jwks_file existence, and zero values of max_request_bytes/max_object_bytes.
findings.proposed_fix: Implement AG_* env overrides for the documented keys (or correct the doc), and extend validate() with the missing checks (enum for log_format, StreamName::new(default_stream), file existence for jwks_file/tls files, non-zero limits).
reasons: The first line of config.rs ('TOML file + environment overrides') overstates: ServerConfig::load only reads TOML, and the environment supplies secrets by variable name (token_env etc.) plus AG_SERVER_CONFIG for the path. validate() (config.rs:361-435) indeed lacks checks for telemetry.log_format (anything but 'json' silently means text, main.rs:163), repos.default_stream, cors_origins, and zero max_request_bytes/max_object_bytes. These are small but verifiable gaps.

This is a grab bag of low-value items. The 'environment overrides' wording in the config.rs module doc is loose, since only secret-bearing variables are read from the environment, and the missing validation (log_format, burst=0, jwks_file) fails visibly or falls back to harmless defaults. None of it misleads an operator in a way that warrants a fix.
findings.refined_fix: Reword the module doc to 'TOML file; secrets come from environment variables named in the file'. In ServerConfig::validate add: `if !matches!(self.telemetry.log_format.as_str(), "text" | "json") { return bad("telemetry.log_format must be 'text' or 'json'"); }`, `ag_types::StreamName::new(&self.repos.default_stream).map_err(|e| ConfigError::Invalid(format!("repos.default_stream: {e}")))?;`, and `if self.limits.max_request_bytes == 0 || self.limits.max_object_bytes == 0 { return bad("limits.max_request_bytes and limits.max_object_bytes must be positive"); }`. Add the CORS check from finding 20.

findings.excerpt: fn chunks(object_id: String, bytes: Vec<u8>) -> BoxStream<v1::ObjectChunk> {
findings.problem: 'objects.chunked' is advertised as streaming, but both directions are fully buffered: downloads load the whole object (up to 256 MiB) via get_object and then slice it into 1 MiB chunks (copying again with to_vec); uploads accumulate the whole object in ObjectSink.current (objects.rs:19,39) before verification, and HTTP PUT collects the body into a Vec (http.rs:404-414). With max_concurrent_requests = 512 the worst-case memory is ~128 GiB with no global in-flight-bytes budget.
findings.proposed_fix: Stream to/from the ObjectStore with incremental hashing, or add a global byte-budget semaphore sized by config ([limits] max_inflight_object_bytes) and document that chunking is a transport detail.
reasons: Buffering is confirmed, and worse than reported. The HTTP PUT /objects/{id} handler (http.rs:~418-440) disables the default body limit and collects up to limits.max_object_bytes (~256 MiB) into a Vec before `app.dispatch`, so before authentication, the concurrency gate and the rate limiter. An unauthenticated client can therefore force large allocations per connection. gRPC ObjectSink (objects.rs:19-60) and get_object/`chunks()` also hold whole objects, and no global in-flight-bytes budget exists. (The 'advertised as streaming' premise is overstated, since the feature is only named 'chunked'.)

The 'objects.chunked' feature is defined in ag-protocol/src/lib.rs as 'Objects larger than one message are streamed in chunks', a wire-framing guarantee that the implementation honours (1 MiB CHUNK_BYTES). It does not promise constant-memory streaming. Server memory use is bounded per request by max_object_bytes and overall by max_concurrent_requests, both operator-configurable. A global in-flight byte budget would be an enhancement.
findings.refined_fix: First, authenticate before buffering. Move the body collection inside the `dispatch` closure, e.g. `app.dispatch(ing, "objects.put", move |call| async move { a.authorize(&call, &repo, Cap::ObjectsWrite, None).await?; let _permit = a.object_budget.acquire(...).await?; let body = http_body_util::Limited::new(request.into_body(), limit).collect().await.map_err(..)?.to_bytes().to_vec(); a.store_object(&call, &repo, &oid, body).await ... })`. Second, add `limits.max_inflight_object_bytes` and an `object_budget: tokio::sync::Semaphore` in AppState with one permit per KiB. Acquire min(Content-Length, max_object_bytes) before reading and return `unavailable` with retry_after when the budget is exhausted. Apply the same budget to ObjectSink::push and get_object.

findings.excerpt: let size = repo.blob(&e.content).map(|b| b.len() as u64).unwrap_or(0);
findings.problem: resolve_path reads the entire blob (up to 256 MiB) just to report its size, and turns a read/corruption error into size 0 instead of an error; the sibling code uses repo.blob_len for exactly this purpose (tree.rs:40,125).
findings.proposed_fix: Use repo.blob_len(&e.content)? and propagate errors.
reasons: api/tree.rs:76 in resolve_path computes `repo.blob(&e.content).map(|b| b.len() as u64).unwrap_or(0)`, which reads and verifies the whole blob (up to 256 MiB) just to report a size, and turns a missing or corrupt blob into size 0. The sibling code in the same file (tree_page, list_directory) uses repo.blob_len for exactly this. resolve_path is a TreeRead route.

api/tree.rs:76 `repo.blob(&e.content).map(|b| b.len() as u64).unwrap_or(0)` reads and verifies the whole blob (up to 256 MiB) just to report its size, and turns any read or corruption error into size 0. The sibling code in the same file (tree_page line 38, list_directory line 114) correctly uses repo.blob_len. Any reader can trigger large reads with resolve_path.
findings.refined_fix: Replace the line with `let size = repo.blob_len(&e.content)?.unwrap_or(0);`, matching tree_page, so only metadata is read and storage errors propagate (as `internal`) instead of reporting size 0. Add a test where the blob is removed from the object store and resolve_path returns an error or an explicit missing indication rather than size 0.

findings.excerpt: | Limits on blobs, ops, DAG depth, requests | ✅ request size, concurrency, per-credential rate limits and repository quotas on the server |
findings.problem: Marks repository quotas as fully done, but per-repo max_object_bytes is not enforced, workspace writes bypass the object quota, quotas are non-atomic, and defaults for most quota fields are not configurable (see findings above). docs/architecture/security.md:72 (the 'Availability' known-limit says there is no rate limiting or quota system, 'those belong to the server') and its 'planned server mode' text in the Known limits section are stale in the other direction: the server exists and none of its authn/authz/rate-limit/quota controls appear in the Controls table.
findings.proposed_fix: Downgrade the traceability row to partial until the quota findings are fixed, and update docs/architecture/security.md to list the server controls (authn, RBAC, scope attenuation, rate limiting, quotas, TLS) with their tests and real limits.
reasons: docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:89 marks 'repository quotas on the server' as fully done (✅), but findings 2 and 3 show that the per-repo max_object_bytes is never enforced and that workspace writes bypass the object quota, and finding 4 shows that the other quotas race. docs/architecture/security.md:59-60 still says identity enforcement 'requires the planned server mode', although ag-server exists, and its Controls table lists no server controls. The 'Availability' bullet (line 72) saying quotas 'belong to the server' is not itself wrong.

Two doc problems are verified. docs/architecture/security.md:58-60 says that enforcing identities 'requires the planned server mode', but ag-server exists and its controls are described in adr-traceability.md and agwp-v1.md. docs/architecture/adr-traceability.md:89 lists 'repository quotas on the server' as fully done, although findings 2 and 3 show workspace writes bypass the object quota and Quota.max_object_bytes is never enforced. The security.md Availability bullet ('no rate limiting or quota system (those belong to the server)') is accurate for local mode.
findings.refined_fix: Change the adr-traceability.md:89 row to 🟡 with text such as 'request size, concurrency, per-credential rate limits and a repository total-bytes quota (upload path only; per-object limit and workspace writes not yet enforced)', and flip it back to ✅ when findings 2-4 land. In security.md replace 'the planned server mode' with 'ag-server (authentication, scoped credentials)' in the known-limits text, and add rows for server authn, RBAC, scope attenuation, rate limiting and quotas to the Controls table, each pointing at its test in crates/ag-server/tests/security.rs.

findings.problem: The topic filter is applied in Rust after reading only limit*4 (1024) audit rows. If none of those rows match the topics, the subscriber cursor is moved to the log's latest_seq, so matching events that sit beyond the 1024-row window are skipped permanently. replay() has the same root cause: it returns an empty page with latest_seq, so a client believes it is caught up. This breaks the documented guarantee 'A subscriber that was away loses nothing' (docs/protocol/agwp-v1.md events section) for any topic-filtered feed during bursts of non-matching events (job.claim, lease.acquire, ...).
findings.proposed_fix: Filter by topic in SQL (audit_after_topics(after_seq, topics, limit) with action = t OR action LIKE t || '.%') or loop in events_after until limit matches are found or the log is exhausted; only advance the cursor to the last row actually scanned, never to latest_seq. Add a test with >1024 non-matching events followed by one matching event and assert delivery over both SSE and replay.
reasons: api/events.rs events_after reads only limit*4 audit rows (256*4=1024 in subscribe), filters in Rust, and the subscribe loop then does `st.cursor = batch.latest_seq` when nothing matched, so matches beyond the window are skipped; replay() returns the same empty page plus latest_seq. Both are reachable from the SSE route and GET /events/replay.

Confirmed in events.rs: events_after reads only limit*4 rows via audit_after, and subscribe sets cursor = batch.latest_seq when nothing in that window matches the topics, so later matching rows are skipped for good. Replay returns an empty page with latest_seq, which the proto says means nothing remains. The audit log holds every job.claim/lease/stream event, so a topic-filtered feed on a mature repo (more than about 2000 earlier non-matching rows) hits this. The existing tests only use a handful of events.
findings.refined_fix: In events_after, loop inside the same `r.meta().read`: `tx.audit_after(cursor, 1024)` page by page, examine each entry (record `scanned = e.seq`), push `to_event` when `matches_topics`, stop as soon as `events.len() == limit` (scanned = that event's seq) or when a page is shorter than 1024 (log exhausted). Add `pub scanned_seq: u64` to EventBatch (highest seq actually examined, else after_seq). In subscribe replace `else if batch.latest_seq > st.cursor { st.cursor = batch.latest_seq; }` with `st.cursor = st.cursor.max(batch.scanned_seq);`. replay() keeps `latest_seq`, but an empty page now truly means no matching event up to it. Test: append >1024 non-matching audit rows then one matching row and assert delivery via both subscribe and replay.

findings.excerpt: scope: serde_json::from_str(&scope_json).unwrap_or_default(),
findings.problem: (Adjacent area: control plane, reported because every API call depends on it.) If a stored credential's scope_json fails to parse, the error is swallowed and the default Scope (no repo/stream/operation restriction) is used, so a corrupted narrow credential silently becomes a fully unrestricted one. Fail-open on a security attenuation.
findings.proposed_fix: Return an error (internal, logged) from row_to_credential and make authenticate_token reject the credential (fail closed). Add a test inserting garbage scope_json and asserting authentication fails.
reasons: The code is now control/mod.rs:306 (credential_from): `scope: serde_json::from_str(r.str(5)?).unwrap_or_default()`. An empty CredentialScope means unrestricted (Scope::is_unrestricted in authz.rs), and credential_from backs authenticate_token on every token request, so an unparsable scope_json fails open. It needs a corrupt or hand-edited row, because v1 types use `#[serde(default)]` without deny_unknown_fields, so version skew does not trigger it. Severity is closer to medium (defence in depth).

Confirmed at control/mod.rs:306: `serde_json::from_str(r.str(5)?).unwrap_or_default()`. A scope_json that fails to parse becomes the default CredentialScope, which Scope::from_wire turns into an unrestricted scope. authenticate_token and may_manage_credential then grant full access. This fails open on a security attenuation, while the same pipeline fails closed on invalid patterns (from_wire returns invalid).
findings.refined_fix: In crates/ag-server/src/control/mod.rs credential_from: `let id = r.string(0)?; ... scope: serde_json::from_str(r.str(5)?).map_err(|e| MetaError::Corrupt(format!("credential {id} has an unreadable scope: {e}")))?,` so `Control::credential()` returns an error and authenticate_token fails closed (internal error, logged). Add a control test that writes garbage scope_json with raw SQL and asserts `credential()` errors and authentication is refused.

findings.excerpt: quota: serde_json::from_str(&quota).unwrap_or_default(),
findings.problem: (Adjacent area.) A repository row whose quota_json cannot be parsed silently gets the default Quota, which is 'unlimited' for every field, instead of surfacing corruption. Together with proposals.rs:16 / streams.rs:36 (`.map(...).unwrap_or(0)`) quota enforcement fails open.
findings.proposed_fix: Propagate the parse error as an internal error; treat a missing repo row in create_proposal/create_stream as not_found instead of 'no quota'.
reasons: control/mod.rs:450 repo_from uses `serde_json::from_str(r.str(6)?).unwrap_or_default()`, and the default Quota is all zeros (unlimited), so a corrupt quota_json silently disables quotas for that repository. The 'missing repo row' half is harmless: create_proposal/create_stream call with_repo_mut right after, which reports not_found for an unknown repo. Needs corrupt data, so low severity.

Only partly valid. control/mod.rs:450 does `serde_json::from_str(r.str(6)?).unwrap_or_default()`, so an unparsable quota_json becomes an all-zero (unlimited) Quota. The 'missing repo row means no quota' half is refuted: with_repo_mut/authorize return not_found for an unknown repository, so `.unwrap_or(0)` in proposals.rs:16 and streams.rs:36 never lets a request through. The same shared control DB can be written by another replica, so a parse failure is plausible.
findings.refined_fix: In repo_from: `let name = r.string(0)?; ... quota: serde_json::from_str(r.str(6)?).map_err(|e| MetaError::Corrupt(format!("repository '{name}' has an unreadable quota: {e}")))?,` (bind `name` first, then use it in the struct). Add a test with garbage quota_json asserting `Control::repo()` errors.

findings.excerpt:
meta_backend: "sqlite".into(),
        object_backend: "fs".into(),
findings.problem: row_to_wire hardcodes the storage backends (and stream_count: 0, changeset_count: 0, durability: ""). Only describe_repo overwrites them. create_repo and list_repos therefore report sqlite/fs even when the server is configured for PostgreSQL + S3 (the shipped Compose config) - wrong data presented as real.
findings.proposed_fix: Derive the backend names from self.cfg.repos.storage (or persist them in RepoRow at creation) in one helper used by create/list/describe; for list_repos either omit the counters/durability or document them as describe-only. Test against a Postgres+S3 config that list and create report postgres/s3.
reasons: repository.rs row_to_wire hardcodes meta_backend "sqlite" and object_backend "fs"; create_repo and list_repos return it unchanged and only describe_repo overwrites it from repo.config().storage(). proto Repo documents these fields as 'Storage in use', and repos.rs derive_storage shows PostgreSQL/S3 repos are created from the configured template, so create/list report wrong backends.

Confirmed: repository.rs:21-22 hardcodes meta_backend="sqlite" and object_backend="fs" in row_to_wire. create_repo and list_repos return it unchanged, and only describe_repo overwrites it from the opened repository's config. The proto says these fields report the 'Storage in use', and it only exempts the counts from list. With the shipped PostgreSQL+S3 template, create and list report the wrong storage.
findings.refined_fix: In repos.rs next to `config_is_shared` add `pub fn storage_backends(config_json: &str) -> (&'static str, &'static str)` that parses `RepoConfig` and returns ("postgres"|"sqlite", "s3"|"fs"), falling back to ("sqlite","fs") when config_json is empty or unparsable. Use it in row_to_wire with `&r.config_json` and reuse it in describe_repo. Keep stream_count/changeset_count/durability as describe-only, which the proto comment already says. Test with a Postgres+S3 config that create and list report postgres/s3.

findings.excerpt:
.and_then(|v| serde_json::from_value::<Outcome>(v.clone()).ok())
.unwrap_or(Outcome::Invalid { reason: format!("operation is {} and has no result yet", i.state) });
findings.problem: get_operation for an integrate operation that is still pending/prepared (exactly the case clients hit after deadline_exceeded, when the docs tell them to 'ask for the outcome') returns a synthetic IntegrationOutcome with status "invalid", which is a terminal documented outcome. A result that fails to deserialize (corruption, version skew) is reported the same way, hiding the error.
findings.proposed_fix: Leave `integration.outcome` unset (or add an explicit "pending" status in the proto) while the operation has no result; return an internal error with the serde cause when a stored result does not deserialize. Test get_operation on an operation interrupted by a failpoint.
reasons: convert.rs operation(): for kind "integrate" a missing result (pending/prepared, the state clients query after deadline_exceeded) or an undecodable one becomes `Outcome::Invalid{reason: "operation is … and has no result yet"}`, so outcome.status reads "invalid", a terminal documented outcome. `.ok()` also hides deserialization errors. IntegrationResult.state does carry the real state, but the outcome is still wrong. The only caller is get_operation in objects.rs.

Confirmed at convert.rs:303-307. An integrate operation with no result yet (pending/prepared, the case after deadline_exceeded) is returned with a made-up IntegrationOutcome status "invalid". A stored result that fails to deserialize is mapped to the same terminal-looking status. The `state` field does carry the real state, but a client reading outcome.status sees a terminal error that never happened, and corruption is hidden. The engine's integration_result does the same.
findings.refined_fix: Change `convert::operation` to return `ApiResult<v1::Operation>`. For "integrate": `let outcome = match i.result.as_ref() { None => None, Some(v) => Some(self::outcome(&serde_json::from_value::<Outcome>(v.clone()).map_err(|e| ApiError::internal(format!("operation {} has an unreadable result: {e}", i.operation_id)))?)) };` and set `outcome` to that Option, so no synthetic result while pending. Update the one caller (`get_operation`, objects.rs ~215) to use `?`. Test get_operation on an operation stopped by a failpoint.

findings.excerpt: let max = self.app.cfg.limits.max_object_bytes;   (and repository.rs:34 `max_object_bytes: 0,`)
findings.problem: The per-repository Quota has max_object_bytes (proto Quota.max_object_bytes, settable through repo.configure; docs say 'a repository may carry a quota of its own'), but it is never read: uploads (grpc ObjectSink and HTTP PUT) only enforce the global cfg.limits.max_object_bytes. Quota.max_streams, max_open_proposals, max_total_object_bytes and requests_per_second/burst are enforced; this one is silently ignored.
findings.proposed_fix: Read the repo's quota in upload_sink/store_object and reject objects larger than min(global, quota.max_object_bytes) when it is > 0 (TooLarge / QuotaExceeded). Add a test configuring a 1 KiB repo quota and uploading 2 KiB.
reasons: Quota.max_object_bytes exists in proto/agwp.proto (field 2) and is settable via repo configure. A grep of crates/ag-server/src shows it is only set to 0 in repository.rs:34 and never read. ObjectSink::push and the HTTP PUT limit (http.rs:421) use only cfg.limits.max_object_bytes, so the per-repository limit is silently ignored.

Confirmed. Quota.max_object_bytes exists in the proto, is settable through repo.configure, and is documented as a per-repository quota. grep shows it is never read: objects.rs:41 and http.rs:421 use only cfg.limits.max_object_bytes, and repository.rs:34 always creates repos with 0. An operator who sets a per-repo object size limit gets silent no-enforcement, unlike the other quota fields.
findings.refined_fix: In store_object read `quota = self.repo_row(repo).await?.map(|r| (r.quota.max_total_object_bytes, r.quota.max_object_bytes, r.object_bytes))` and, inside the with_repo_mut closure after authorization, reject with `ApiError::new(ErrorCode::TooLarge, ...)` when `per_object > 0 && size > per_object`. In `upload_sink`, after `authorize`, load the repo row once and keep `min(global, per_repo)` in the ObjectSink so `push` rejects early. Test: set a 1 KiB per-repo quota via configure and upload 2 KiB over gRPC and HTTP PUT.

findings.problem: The quota check uses a snapshot of object_bytes read before the engine call (and via a blocking SQLite call on the async worker); concurrent uploads each see the same `used`, so a repository can exceed max_total_object_bytes by (concurrency x object size). The counter itself is updated in a separate step after the put, so a crash leaves it permanently off ('approximate' per control.rs).
findings.proposed_fix: Reserve bytes atomically in the control DB (UPDATE repos SET object_bytes = object_bytes + ?size WHERE name = ? AND (?max = 0 OR object_bytes + ?size <= ?max)), roll back on failure, run it in spawn_blocking, and let gc/fsck recount. Add a concurrent-upload test.
reasons: objects.rs store_object reads `r.object_bytes` into `quota` before with_repo_mut and compares `used + size > max_total` inside the closure. Concurrent uploads therefore all see the same `used`, and the counter is bumped by a separate `control.add_object_bytes` after the put, so the quota can be overshot. The 'blocking SQLite on the async worker' part is wrong: repo_row uses spawn_blocking.

The counter is documented as approximate: control/mod.rs:120 says 'Tracked object bytes (approximate; recomputed by maintenance)', and gc resets it with set_object_bytes. It is a soft quota, so the small concurrent overshoot is an accepted, documented limitation. The claim of a blocking SQLite call on the async worker is wrong: store_object reads the row through App::repo_row, which uses spawn_blocking.
